Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Let a slightly nonspherical cloud fall Shape changes the directional gravitational field even at fixed initial density. Consider an isolated, homogeneous, nonrotating pressure-free spheroid: no expansion, magnetic field, turbulence, or shocks. Follow it only before an axis collapses. A spheroid is a shape; it does not imply that the cloud rotates. a₁ = a₂ = a(t), a₃ = c(t), q = c/a M = (4π/3)ρa²c = constant ρ(t)/ρ₀ = a₀²c₀/[a(t)²c(t)] Use the homologous velocity field vᵢ = (ȧᵢ/aᵢ)xᵢ. The interior gravitational acceleration of a homogeneous ellipsoid is also linear in xᵢ, so this gives a self-consistent homogeneous evolution before caustics. It is not an exact description of arbitrary nonuniform clouds. 02From gravitational coefficients to axis motion Use the coefficients Aᵢ from the ellipsoidal-potential chapter. Inside the cloud gᵢ = −2πGρAᵢxᵢ and their sum is two. Applying the pressure-free equation of motion to surface elements produces two ordinary differential equations. Aᵢ = a₁a₂a₃∫₀∞du/[(aᵢ²+u)√((a₁²+u)(a₂²+u)(a₃²+u))] 2Aₐ+Ac = 2 ä = −2πGρAₐa, c̈ = −2πGρAcc For oblate q < 1 use e = √(1−q²); for prolate q > 1 use e = √(1−q⁻²). Use series near the sphere to avoid cancellation. The acceleration includes the axis length as well as its gravitational coefficient. q < 1: Ac = 2[1−q arccos(q)/e]/e² q > 1: Ac = (1−e²)[ln((1+e)/(1−e))−2e]/e³ q = 1: Aₐ = Ac = 2/3, Aₐ = (2−Ac)/2 03Specify initial conditions and a time unit Use a₀ as the length unit and t₀ = (2πGρ₀)⁻¹/² as the time unit. The dimensionless initial conditions are a = 1, c = q₀, with both velocities zero. Primes denote derivatives with respect to dimensionless time τ. D = ρ/ρ₀ = q₀/(a²c) a″ = −DAₐa, c″ = −DAcc Changing the initial density rescales physical time by ρ₀⁻¹/². Varying q₀ at fixed a₀ and initial density also changes the mass. The panel integrates this stated family; it does not allow arbitrary initial contraction velocities or external pressures. 04Check against spherical collapse and energy conservation For a sphere, a = c = b and b″ = −2/(3b²). The initially stationary solution has the parametric form below, providing an independent numerical benchmark. b = (1+cosη)/2, τ = (√3/4)(η+sinη) τff = π√3/4, tff = √[3π/(32Gρ₀)] Total energy supplies a second check. The mean squared coordinate along an axis is aᵢ²/5, which determines the kinetic energy per unit mass. Combine it with the potential-energy integral to obtain a dimensionless invariant. ℋ = (2a′²+c′²)/10 − (q₀/5)I(a,c) I = ∫₀∞du/[(a²+u)√(c²+u)] q < 1: I = 2 arccos(q)/(a√(1−q²)) q > 1: I = 2 arcosh(q)/(a√(q²−1)) Oblate clouds flatten further; prolate clouds become more elongated. A vanishing axis makes the density diverge and ends the smooth homogeneous flow. Stop when either the smallest initial-normalized axis or the current short/long axis ratio reaches 0.03. This is a numerical cutoff, not a measured singularity time. 05Follow shape and density Teaching plots integrate the axis equations; they do not reproduce a particular original figure or particle simulation. Assumptions differ from pressure-supported Shu collapse and from the pre-crossing Zel’dovich approximation. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed initial shape, quadruple the initial density. What happens to the physical time needed to reach the same shape? Show the answer and reasoning The time unit (2πGρ₀)⁻¹/² halves. With the same dimensionless initial velocities, the dimensionless track is unchanged and physical times halve. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
